title: UNIT 4: CHEMICAL KINETICS
notes:
✓ Chemical kinetics → The branch of chemistry concerned with the rates and mechanisms of chemical reactions.
Chemical reactions occur at different speeds: some are very fast, while others may take days, years, or even longer.
✓ Reaction rate → Describes how quickly reactants are consumed or products are formed.

title: 4.1 Introduction
notes:
Chemical reactions do not all proceed at the same rate. Combustion reactions may occur within seconds, while processes such as rusting, weathering, and decomposition of some materials can be much slower.

✓ Chemical kinetics → Studies the speed of chemical reactions and the factors that control their rates.
Understanding reaction rates is important for controlling chemical processes, improving industrial production, preserving food, and understanding chemical changes in everyday life.

title: 4.2 The Rate of a Reaction
notes:
✓ Rate of a chemical reaction → The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.

For a reaction:
Reactants → Products

The concentration of reactants decreases as the reaction proceeds, while the concentration of products increases.

✓ Rate = Change in concentration / Change in time

For a reactant:
✓ Rate = −Δ[Reactant]/Δt

For a product:
✓ Rate = Δ[Product]/Δt

✓ Usual units of reaction rate → mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

title: 4.2.1 Rate and Reaction Progress
notes:
The progress of a reaction can be followed by measuring the concentration of a reactant or product at different times.

✓ Concentration-time graph → The slope represents the rate of concentration change.

At the beginning of many reactions, the rate is relatively high because reactant concentrations are greatest. As reactants are consumed, their concentrations decrease and the reaction rate generally becomes slower.

→ Concentration-time curve becomes less steep as the reaction proceeds.

title: 4.2.2 Rate Expressions and Stoichiometry
notes:
For reactions involving different stoichiometric coefficients, the rate must be related to the coefficients of the balanced chemical equation.

For:
aA + bB → cC + dD

✓ Rate = −1/a Δ[A]/Δt = −1/b Δ[B]/Δt = 1/c Δ[C]/Δt = 1/d Δ[D]/Δt

The coefficients ensure that the same reaction rate is obtained regardless of which reactant or product is used.

◆ EXAMPLE
2A → B
✓ Rate = −½ Δ[A]/Δt = Δ[B]/Δt

→ The negative sign is used for reactants because their concentrations decrease.

title: 4.2.3 Average Rate
notes:
✓ Average rate → The change in concentration over a specified time interval.

✓ Average rate = −Δ[Reactant]/Δt
✓ Average rate = Δ[Product]/Δt

It describes the overall rate during a particular period rather than the rate at one exact moment.

◆ EXAMPLE
If the concentration of a reactant changes from [A]₁ to [A]₂ during the time interval t₁ to t₂:

✓ Average rate = −([A]₂ − [A]₁)/(t₂ − t₁)

→ Because a reactant concentration decreases, the negative sign gives a positive rate.

title: 4.2.4 Instantaneous Rate
notes:
✓ Instantaneous rate → The rate of a reaction at a particular moment in time.

It can be determined from the slope of a tangent drawn to a concentration-versus-time curve at the required point.

✓ Instantaneous rate = Slope of tangent to the concentration-time graph.

The instantaneous rate usually changes as a reaction proceeds because the concentrations of reactants and products change.

title: 4.2.5 Initial Rate
notes:
✓ Initial rate → The instantaneous rate of a reaction at the beginning of the reaction, when t is approximately zero.

It is obtained from the slope of the tangent to the concentration-time curve at the initial point.

Initial rates are useful for studying how changes in reaction conditions affect reaction speed because the concentrations of the reactants are known at the beginning and the effects of products are minimal.

title: 4.2.6 Conditions Needed for a Chemical Reaction
notes:
Chemical reactions are explained using collision theory. Reacting particles must collide before a reaction can occur.

However, not every collision produces a reaction. A collision is effective only when the particles collide with sufficient energy and the proper orientation.

◆ CONDITIONS FOR A SUCCESSFUL REACTION
✓ Collision between reacting particles.
✓ Proper orientation of the particles.
✓ Sufficient energy to overcome the activation energy.

→ More frequent effective collisions generally produce a faster reaction.

title: 4.2.7 Collision Theory
notes:
✓ Collision theory → Chemical reactions occur when atoms, ions, or molecules collide with one another.

The rate of reaction is related to the frequency of collisions and the number of effective collisions.

◆ EFFECTIVE COLLISION
✓ Collision that has sufficient energy and proper orientation to produce products.

◆ INEFFECTIVE COLLISION
✓ Collision that does not produce products because the particles lack sufficient energy, have an unsuitable orientation, or both.

→ Increasing the number of effective collisions increases the reaction rate.

title: 4.2.8 Proper Orientation
notes:
Reacting particles must collide in an appropriate orientation for the required bonds to break and new bonds to form.

Even when particles collide with sufficient energy, a reaction may not occur if the atoms or reactive parts of the molecules are not correctly oriented.

✓ Effective collision requires → Sufficient collision energy + proper orientation.

title: 4.2.9 Activation Energy
notes:
✓ Activation energy (Eₐ) → The minimum energy that reacting particles must possess for an effective collision to occur and a chemical reaction to proceed.

Particles with energy below the activation energy generally do not react when they collide.

Increasing temperature increases the average kinetic energy of particles and increases the number of particles with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. This generally increases the reaction rate.

→ Higher activation energy generally means a slower reaction than a similar reaction with lower activation energy under the same conditions.

title: 4.3 Factors Affecting the Rate of a Chemical Reaction
notes:
◆ MAIN FACTORS
✓ Nature of the reactants.
✓ Surface area of the reactants.
✓ Concentration of the reactants.
✓ Temperature.
✓ Presence of a catalyst or inhibitor.

→ These factors change either the frequency of collisions, the energy of collisions, the number of effective collisions, or the pathway by which the reaction occurs.

title: 4.3.1 Nature of Reactants
notes:
✓ Nature of reactants → Affects reaction rate because different substances have different tendencies to react due to differences in their atoms, ions, bonds, and structures.

Reactions between ions in aqueous solution can be very rapid because the reacting ions can interact directly. Other reactions require the breaking and reorganizing of strong covalent bonds and may proceed more slowly.

◆ EXAMPLES
→ Sodium reacts with water much more rapidly than calcium.
→ Iron reacts much more slowly with air than sodium.

title: 4.3.2 Surface Area of Reactants
notes:
For reactions involving a solid and another phase, increasing the surface area of the solid generally increases the reaction rate.

A powdered solid exposes more particles to the other reactant than the same mass in large pieces. This provides more contact area and increases the frequency of collisions.

✓ Greater surface area → More contact between reactants → More collisions → Faster reaction.

◆ EXAMPLE
Powdered calcium carbonate reacts with acid faster than large pieces of calcium carbonate.

title: 4.3.3 Concentration of Reactants
notes:
At constant temperature, increasing the concentration of reactants generally increases the reaction rate.

✓ Higher concentration → More reacting particles in a given volume → More frequent collisions → More effective collisions per unit time.

For gases, increasing pressure can increase the effective concentration of the gases and may increase the reaction rate.

→ Pressure changes generally have little effect on reactions involving only solids or liquids.

title: 4.3.4 Temperature of Reactants
notes:
Increasing temperature generally increases the rate of a chemical reaction.

Higher temperature gives reacting particles greater average kinetic energy. The particles move faster, collide more frequently, and a larger fraction of collisions have enough energy to overcome the activation energy.

✓ Temperature ↑ → Average kinetic energy ↑ → Effective collisions ↑ → Reaction rate generally ↑.

In many cases, a relatively small increase in temperature can produce a significant increase in reaction rate.

title: 4.3.5 Catalysts
notes:
✓ Catalyst → A substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

◆ PROPERTIES OF A CATALYST
✓ Increases reaction rate when it is a positive catalyst.
✓ Provides a pathway with lower activation energy.
✓ Is not consumed overall in the reaction.
✓ Can be recovered after the reaction.
✓ Does not change the equilibrium position of a reversible reaction.

→ Lower activation energy allows a greater fraction of collisions to become effective.

title: 4.3.6 Positive Catalysts
notes:
✓ Positive catalyst → A catalyst that increases the rate of a chemical reaction by providing a pathway with lower activation energy.

◆ EXAMPLE
Vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅, acts as a catalyst in:

2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g)

→ The catalyst increases the rate without being consumed overall.

Catalysts are important in industrial processes because they can allow reactions to proceed at useful rates under practical conditions.

title: 4.3.7 Negative Catalysts or Inhibitors
notes:
✓ Negative catalyst or inhibitor → A substance that decreases the rate of a chemical reaction.

The textbook describes this as occurring through an increase in the effective activation energy or by interfering with the reaction pathway.

◆ EXAMPLE
OH⁻ can act as an inhibitor in:

OCl⁻(aq) + I⁻(aq) → OI⁻(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

→ Inhibitors are useful when a reaction needs to be slowed down or controlled.

title: 4.3.8 Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Catalysts
notes:
Catalysts can be classified according to their physical state relative to the reactants.

◆ HOMOGENEOUS CATALYST
✓ Catalyst and reacting substances are in the same physical state.

◆ HETEROGENEOUS CATALYST
✓ Catalyst and reacting substances are in different physical states.

Catalysts can be highly specific. A catalyst that is effective for one reaction may have little or no effect on another reaction.

✓ Enzymes → Biological catalysts that control many reactions in living organisms.

title: UNIT 4 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ CHEMICAL KINETICS → Study of reaction rates and reaction mechanisms.

✓ REACTION RATE → Change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
✓ REACTANT RATE → −Δ[Reactant]/Δt.
✓ PRODUCT RATE → Δ[Product]/Δt.
✓ AVERAGE RATE → Rate measured over a specified time interval.
✓ INSTANTANEOUS RATE → Rate at a particular moment; obtained from the tangent slope of a concentration-time graph.
✓ INITIAL RATE → Instantaneous rate at the beginning of a reaction.

◆ COLLISION THEORY
✓ Reacting particles must collide for a reaction to occur.
✓ EFFECTIVE COLLISION → Collision with sufficient energy and proper orientation that produces products.
✓ ACTIVATION ENERGY (Eₐ) → Minimum energy required for an effective reaction.

◆ MAIN FACTORS
✓ Nature of reactants.
✓ Surface area.
✓ Concentration.
✓ Temperature.
✓ Catalysts or inhibitors.

✓ Surface area ↑ → Collision frequency ↑ → Rate ↑.
✓ Concentration ↑ → Collision frequency ↑ → Rate generally ↑.
✓ Temperature ↑ → Average kinetic energy ↑ and effective collisions ↑ → Rate generally ↑.
✓ Positive catalyst → Lowers activation energy and increases reaction rate.
✓ Inhibitor → Decreases reaction rate.
✓ Catalyst → Changes the reaction pathway but does not change the equilibrium position.

✓ KEY IDEA → Reaction rate depends on how frequently reacting particles collide and how many of those collisions are effective.
